title: Two Roads to Persuasion
objective: After this level you can explain the central and peripheral routes to persuasion and when each one works.
summary: Messages persuade by their arguments (the central route) or by cues like who is speaking (the peripheral route). Students affected by a proposal weighed its arguments; others followed the source.

cards.headline: Same speech, same speaker. One date decided what mattered.
cards.body: In 1981, psychologists played students a speech proposing a tough new exam for seniors. Some heard strong arguments, some weak ones; some were told it came from experts, some from a high school class. What students cared about depended on when the exam would start.

cards.headline: Two roads
cards.body: Persuasion is changing an attitude through communication. Richard Petty and John Cacioppo's elaboration likelihood model says it travels two roads. The central route runs through thoughtful consideration of the arguments. The peripheral route runs through cues around the message, like an attractive speaker or a celebrity endorsement.

cards.headline: The exam experiment
cards.body: In the 1981 experiment by Petty, Cacioppo and Rachel Goldman, University of Missouri students heard a message proposing senior comprehensive exams. The arguments were strong or weak. The source was said to be a commission chaired by a Princeton professor, or a local high school class. Half were told the exams would start next year; half, in 10 years.

cards.headline: Care, and you check the arguments
cards.body: When the exams would start the following year, landing on the students themselves, their attitudes depended mainly on argument quality. When the exams were 10 years away, attitudes depended mainly on the source's expertise. The central route works when people are motivated and able to think, and it tends to produce lasting change; peripheral-route change is usually less permanent.

cards.headline: Two roads
learned: Central route: the quality of the arguments
Peripheral route: cues like attractiveness or celebrity
If it affected them, students weighed the arguments
Central-route change tends to last longer

questions.prompt: The route to persuasion that relies on cues such as a celebrity endorsement, rather than the arguments, is _____.

options.label: the central route
options.rationale: That route runs through the arguments themselves.

options.label: the normative route
options.rationale: That's a kind of social influence, not a route in this model.

options.label: the dissonance route
options.rationale: Dissonance is a separate idea about inner conflict.

questions.explanation: The peripheral route works through cues around the message, such as an attractive speaker or a celebrity.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the persuasion research with its description.
questions.explanation: Petty and Cacioppo proposed the elaboration likelihood model. When the exams would start the following year, attitudes depended on argument quality; when they were 10 years away, on the source's expertise.

questions.prompt: Cognitive science pictures the mind as an information processor. In that picture, what mainly separates the central route from the peripheral one?

options.label: How carefully the message's arguments are processed
Whether the message is spoken aloud or written down
options.rationale: The model is about processing, not the medium.

options.label: Whether the listener is rewarded for agreeing
options.rationale: That's a behaviorist framing, not this model.

questions.explanation: The central route means working through the arguments carefully; the peripheral route leans on cues with little processing.
